title: US Serves Pannun Lawsuit Papers on India; Court Clears Delhi Route for Doval Summons
excerpt: The State Department transmitted the summons to the Indian Embassy on October 9 and told the court it takes no position on the claims, as the MEA rejected the suit as frivolous.
body:
• The US State Department has transmitted the summons and complaint in Gurpatwant Singh Pannun's civil lawsuit to the Indian Embassy in Washington, and told the New York court the papers were delivered on October 9, 2026.
  • A federal judge on November 9 allowed Pannun to pursue service on National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and former RAW chief Samant Goel through courts in Delhi, with a November 30 deadline to file the proposed procedure.
  • India's Ministry of External Affairs on November 10 rejected the suit as frivolous and said service of judicial documents in India can only be routed through the Ministry of Law and Justice, the designated central authority.
  • The State Department stressed that transmitting the papers was a procedural requirement and does not mean the US government supports Pannun's allegations.

The United States has formally served the Indian government with papers in a civil lawsuit filed by Sikh separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, while a New York court has cleared a separate route to serve two of India's most senior security officials through courts in Delhi. The twin developments move a case India calls frivolous into a new procedural phase, without any finding on the allegations themselves.

According to reporting on the court filings, the State Department transmitted a diplomatic note containing the summons and complaint to the Indian Embassy in Washington on October 9, 2026, and later informed the US District Court for the Southern District of New York that the papers had been delivered. The department clarified that transmitting legal documents was a legal and procedural requirement, and that it took no position on the claims in the suit.

Service on Doval and Goel through Delhi courts

In a separate order on November 9, a federal judge permitted Pannun to pursue service on National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and former Research and Analysis Wing chief Samant Goel through Indian courts, under the Hague Convention framework for serving judicial documents abroad and relevant provisions of India's Code of Civil Procedure. The order does not mean Doval or Goel have personally received the summonses. Pannun has been directed to submit the necessary documents and the proposed procedure for the court's approval by November 30, 2026.

What the lawsuit alleges

Pannun filed the civil suit in September 2024. It alleges a conspiracy to assassinate him in the United States in 2023, and names the Government of India, Doval, Goel, former RAW officer Vikash Yadav, Indian national Nikhil Gupta and several unidentified defendants. The civil case is connected to a separate US criminal investigation into an alleged murder-for-hire plot, in which Gupta was arrested in the Czech Republic in 2023. The allegations in the civil suit have not been established in court, and India has consistently rejected claims of official involvement in any attempt on Pannun's life.

India's response

At a media briefing in New Delhi on Tuesday, Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal rejected the suit outright.

"We reject the fabricated and malicious attacks on our high officials. As also, we reject the frivolous lawsuits. A request for the service of judicial documents in India can only be routed through India's designated central authority, which is the Ministry of Law and Justice."

— Randhir Jaiswal, MEA spokesperson, via IANS

Jaiswal's point goes to procedure as much as to substance: New Delhi is signalling that any service inside India must travel through the central authority channel, not through arrangements made directly by the plaintiff's lawyers.

What happens next

The immediate deadline is November 30, when Pannun must file the documents and proposed procedure for serving Doval and Goel through the Delhi courts. Whether India accepts service through its central authority, and how the Southern District of New York handles any objection, will decide whether the case moves toward arguments on the merits or stays in a fight over process. For now, nothing in the latest orders changes the underlying position of either side: Pannun is pressing ahead, and India is refusing to treat the claims as legitimate.
image_caption: National Security Adviser Ajit Doval, who is named as a defendant in the civil lawsuit. A New York judge has allowed service on Doval through courts in Delhi, with a November 30 deadline for the proposed procedure.
nri_angle: The case remains a live irritant in India-US ties watched closely by the Sikh diaspora in North America, where Pannun continues to organise his referendum campaign.
